lesson.title: Talk in binary
lesson.subtitle: Count to 31 on one hand, and see why bits matter

video.title: Talk in binary
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — your computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph in the computer room holds up one hand, fingers spread; then he raises fingers in a quick pattern and grins.
scenes.animation: Fingers count 1 to 5 the usual way, then flick through a binary pattern.
scenes.narration: How high can you count on one hand? Most people say five. I can count to thirty-one. By the end of this video, so can you.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how machines count with only ones and zeros.

scenes.visual: A single switch flips between 1 and 0; then a row of switches appears beside it.
scenes.animation: One switch flips; four more slide in beside it.
scenes.narration: Each switch inside a device is on or off, one or zero: that's a bit. One bit can say only two things: yes or no, light or dark. To say more, you need more bits.

scenes.visual: Five switches in a row, each labelled with its value: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Bars grow above them, each twice as tall as the one to its right.
scenes.animation: Values pop in from right to left; bars grow.
scenes.narration: So each bit gets a value. The bit on the right is worth one, the next two, then four, eight and sixteen: each double the last. To read a number, add up the bits that are on.

scenes.visual: The five switches show 1 0 1 1 0 under their values; the values of the switches that are on light up and add up on a board.
scenes.animation: Switches flip into place; 16, 4 and 2 glow and slide into a sum.
scenes.narration: Let's read one zero one one zero. Sixteen is on, eight is off, four and two are on, one is off. Sixteen plus four plus two: twenty-two.

scenes.visual: A hand, palm out, with 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 over the thumb and fingers; fingers rise one by one until all five are up.
scenes.animation: Values pop over each finger; fingers rise; 31 grows at the end.
scenes.narration: Now your hand. Your thumb is worth one, then two, four, eight, and your little finger sixteen. A finger up is one; down is zero. All five up makes thirty-one!

scenes.visual: Ms Salma at the board, where 11001 is written large. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Here are five bits: one one zero zero one. What number is that?

scenes.visual: 11001 with 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 above it; the 16, 8 and 1 glow and add to 25. A ghost of the number reversed fades out.
scenes.narration: Twenty-five: sixteen plus eight plus one. If you said nineteen, you read it from the wrong end. The biggest value is always on the left.

scenes.visual: Eight switches in a row, grouped by a bracket labelled byte; a counter runs from 0 to 255.
scenes.animation: The bracket draws; the counter spins up.
scenes.narration: Eight bits make a byte. A byte counts from zero to two hundred and fifty-five: two hundred and fifty-six values, enough for every English letter and digit.

scenes.visual: A thermometer, a letter A and an Arabic letter, a phone message and a photo, each with a small stack of bytes that grows taller.
scenes.animation: Each item pops in with its stack.
scenes.narration: Everything a device stores is bytes. A temperature reading takes a few. An English letter takes one, an Arabic letter two. A text message takes about a hundred, and a phone photo about three million.

scenes.visual: Two light meters side by side: one with eight chunky steps, one with a fine smooth scale; a passing cloud moves only the fine one.
scenes.animation: A cloud passes; the fine scale dips slightly, the chunky one doesn't move.
scenes.narration: More bits also mean more detail. A light sensor read with three bits has just eight levels. With ten bits, it has one thousand and twenty-four, so it notices tiny changes.

scenes.visual: A phone's storage bar fills and its data bundle drains as a huge photo is sent; then an engineer picks a small, neat number of bits for a sensor.
scenes.animation: Bars fill and drain; a target badge pops.
scenes.on_screen_text: But more data to keep and send
scenes.narration: But every extra bit costs more memory, more data to send, and more battery. A huge photo looks great, but it eats your data bundle. So engineers choose just enough bits for the job.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside a small sensor with four switches drawn above it. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A small sensor sends each reading with four bits. How many different values can four bits count?

scenes.visual: Four cards line up: doubling values, a byte, a fine scale, a full phone.
scenes.narration: Sixteen, from zero to fifteen: each extra bit doubles it. Remember: each bit is worth double the one on its right, eight bits make a byte, and more bits mean more detail, but more data.

scenes.visual: Two students facing each other, one counting on her fingers, the other ticking numbers in a notebook; a page shows an age written in 1s and 0s.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: count to thirty-one on one hand, with a friend checking. Then write your age in binary. Next time, you'll meet the tiny computer that counts like this.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the bits that are on are worth 16, 8 and 1, and together they make 25.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — read it from the left: 16 + 8 + 1 = 25. You only get 19 if you read it backwards.

checkpoints.prompt: How many different values can 4 bits count?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 4 bits count from 0 to 15, which is 16 values. Each extra bit doubles it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — each bit doubles the count: 2, 4, 8, 16. So 4 bits give 16 values, from 0 to 15.
